idiom_name: single entry function + ordered common-behaviour chain + dispatch table
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: wire the server so exactly one entry point receives every request; inside it run the shared chain (authenticate, resolve session/locale, start tracing, map errors) and then select a handler from a declarative table keyed by method and path. Keep the entry point free of request-specific logic: hand a request context to the handler and let it produce the response. What replaces the classic structure: the FrontController class with its decorated pre/post hooks collapses into one entry function plus an ordered list of wrapping stages, while only the dispatch target - a Command or handler - remains an explicit component per kind of request.
pitfalls: Letting the entry point grow request-specific branches until it becomes the application instead of a dispatcher.
Leaving ordering implicit: authentication that runs before session resolution sees an anonymous principal and silently denies or admits wrongly.
Sharing mutable state between requests in the entry point, which turns a stateless dispatch decision into a concurrency bug.
Adding a short-circuit stage (e.g. OPTIONS CORS preflight) in the wrong position, after protected routes instead of before, causing preflight failures for authenticated endpoints.
Assuming stage ordering is caller-side controllable when in fact it is registration-order dependent; a developer reading the handler code cannot see that auth runs before or after it.
Not handling the case where a downstream handler writes to the response stream before the front controller's error handler runs, leading to 'headers already sent' errors on exceptions.
Leaking resource handles (database connections, file handles) from a stage if an exception occurs before the finally block is reached; use try-finally or resource-adapter stages.
Implementing request-context resolution (e.g. parsing an auth token) inside the same stage as business logic, making the stage impossible to unit-test in isolation without a full HTTP stack.

Wrong move: make every cross-cutting concern an unconstrained middleware that mutates request/response objects -> Y fails -> dependent stages hide their data flow and become order-sensitive -> instead translate HTTP once into explicit inputs and compose constrained functions behind a thin front controller.

Wrong move: treat pipeline registration order as an implementation detail -> Y fails -> a terminal stage can skip later error or audit handling and authentication can run before its session dependency -> instead declare stage dependencies and short-circuit semantics at startup.
sources: Microsoft Learn: Implementing Front Controller in ASP.NET Using HTTPHandler. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/msp-n-p/ff647590(v%3dpandp.10)
